subtopic_detail: Isolated breast development in a toddler with normal growth velocity and unadvanced bone age
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 2-year-old girl referred because of breast development. Her mother noticed 'small lumps under both nipples' at around 18 months and says they have waxed and waned since, being more obvious some weeks than others.

There has been no change in body odour, no acne, no pubic or axillary hair and no vaginal bleeding. She takes no medications and there are no creams, gels or supplements in the house.

On examination she has Tanner stage 2 breast tissue bilaterally with no areolar enlargement or pigmentation, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair and no clitoromegaly. Her height has tracked steadily along the 60th centile across four measurements since 12 months of age, giving a growth velocity of 8 cm per year. A bone age radiograph reports a skeletal age of 2 years 1 month against a chronological age of 2 years 2 months.

data_table.Pubertal staging: Tanner stage 2 breast bilaterally without areolar enlargement, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair, no clitoromegaly
data_table.Growth: Height tracking along the 60th centile across four measurements; growth velocity 8 cm per year
data_table.Imaging: Bone age 2 years 1 month against chronological age 2 years 2 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test and repeat the bone age film
options.rationale: Stimulation testing is used to confirm central activation when the clinical picture already suggests true precocious puberty, meaning progressive staging with accelerated growth and an advanced bone age. Testing a child whose skeletal age matches her chronological age generates cost, distress and false positives without altering management. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary within the next month
options.rationale: Central nervous system imaging is indicated once central precocious puberty has been biochemically confirmed, and the yield is highest in girls under 6 years and in all boys. Imaging a child with no evidence of gonadotrophin activation would require sedation for no diagnostic gain. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist and refer her to endocrinology
options.rationale: Agonist therapy is reserved for confirmed central precocious puberty where rapid progression threatens final adult height or causes psychosocial harm. Suppressing an axis that has not been activated exposes the child to injections and side effects with no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and measure serum oestradiol and the adrenal androgens
options.rationale: Ultrasound and androgen measurement search for a peripheral oestrogen or androgen source such as an ovarian cyst, a McCune-Albright lesion or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, all of which produce virilisation, rapid progression or bleeding. The absence of pubic hair, clitoromegaly, acne and growth acceleration argues strongly against a peripheral source. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her growth and pubertal staging again in six months
options.rationale: Isolated waxing and waning breast tissue in a toddler with no other secondary sexual characteristics, a normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age is premature thelarche, a benign self-limiting variant. Serial review of height velocity and staging is the investigation, because progression over 6 months is what separates thelarche from true precocity. (Source: RCH CPG: Precocious puberty)

explanation.summary: Premature thelarche is isolated breast development, usually appearing between 6 months and 3 years, driven by transient follicular activity in a minipubertal ovary rather than by activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. It is distinguished from true precocious puberty by what is absent as much as by what is present: no pubic or axillary hair, no acne or adult body odour, no growth acceleration and no bone age advance. Bone age is the single most informative investigation because oestrogen exposure sufficient to develop breast tissue over months would also advance the skeleton. Serial observation over 6 months is diagnostic, since thelarche stays static or regresses while true precocity progresses through the Tanner stages. Referral thresholds are breast development before 8 years in girls or testicular enlargement before 9 years in boys when accompanied by growth acceleration or bone age advance.
key_points: Premature thelarche is isolated breast tissue with no other secondary sexual characteristics
Normal growth velocity and a bone age matching chronological age are the reassuring findings
Serial staging and height velocity over 6 months is the diagnostic test
Investigate when there is pubic hair, acne, growth acceleration, bleeding or virilisation
Brain imaging follows biochemical confirmation of central activation, not clinical suspicion alone
explanation.pearls: Areolar enlargement and pigmentation, rather than the size of the breast bud itself, is the physical sign that most reliably marks genuine oestrogen exposure and should prompt investigation even when the bone age is only mildly advanced.

sources.label: Australasian Paediatric Endocrine Group: Puberty disorders

subtopic_detail: Setting for influenza vaccination in a child with previous anaphylaxis to egg
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old boy in early autumn whose parents want him vaccinated against influenza before a family trip.

At 11 months of age he developed generalised urticaria, lip swelling, vomiting and audible wheeze within ten minutes of his first taste of scrambled egg, and was treated with intramuscular adrenaline in an emergency department. Skin prick testing was subsequently positive to egg white and he carries an adrenaline autoinjector.

He has received his measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at 12 months without any reaction. He is well today, has no asthma and has had no recent febrile illness. Your practice has an adrenaline autoinjector, oxygen and a resuscitation trolley, and a second staff member is on site.

data_table.Allergy history: Anaphylaxis to egg at 11 months treated with intramuscular adrenaline; skin prick test positive to egg white
data_table.Vaccine history: Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine at 12 months tolerated without reaction
data_table.Practice resources: Adrenaline autoinjector, oxygen, resuscitation trolley and a second staff member available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer the influenza vaccine in the practice with 15 minutes of observation
options.rationale: Egg allergy of any severity, including previous anaphylaxis, is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination in Australia, because the ovalbumin content of registered vaccines is below the threshold that triggers reactions. Vaccination proceeds in any setting equipped to manage anaphylaxis, with the same standard 15 minute observation applied to every vaccinee. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Refer him to a specialist immunisation clinic for the influenza vaccine in hospital
options.rationale: Specialist immunisation clinic referral is reserved for a documented anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the vaccine itself or to one of its other components such as gelatin or neomycin. Referring for egg allergy alone creates a delay in which the child may miss the season altogether. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Give the influenza vaccine in two divided doses 30 minutes apart in the practice
options.rationale: Graded or split dosing was historical practice abandoned once studies showed no excess reactions with full single doses in egg allergic children. Splitting the dose risks giving an incomplete antigen load and is not a licensed method of administration. (Source: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child)
source_refs: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child

options.text: Withhold the influenza vaccine and rely on vaccination of his household contacts
options.rationale: Cocooning through household vaccination is an adjunct for infants under 6 months who cannot be vaccinated, not a substitute for a child who is eligible. Withholding leaves a preschool child, a group with high influenza hospitalisation rates, unprotected on the basis of a contraindication that does not exist. (Source: The Australian Immunisation Handbook)

options.text: Perform skin prick testing to the influenza vaccine before administering the dose
options.rationale: Skin testing with vaccine is not predictive of clinical reaction and generates irritant false positives that lead to unnecessary withholding. It has a limited role only in evaluating a suspected reaction to a previous dose of the same vaccine. (Source: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child)
source_refs: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child

explanation.summary: Egg allergy has been progressively removed as a barrier to vaccination as ovalbumin content in manufactured vaccines has fallen. Influenza vaccines registered in Australia contain ovalbumin at concentrations far below the threshold associated with reactions, and large studies including children with previous anaphylaxis have found no excess of severe reactions. Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is grown in chick embryo fibroblast culture rather than egg and has never been contraindicated by egg allergy. The two vaccines that do contain clinically relevant quantities of egg protein are yellow fever and Q fever vaccine, and those require allergist assessment before administration. Every vaccinee, allergic or not, is observed for 15 minutes in a setting able to recognise and treat anaphylaxis.
key_points: Egg allergy, including previous anaphylaxis, is not a contraindication to influenza vaccination
Measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is cultured in chick fibroblasts and is safe in egg allergy
Yellow fever and Q fever vaccines do contain relevant egg protein and need specialist assessment
Split or graded dosing has been abandoned and is not a licensed administration method
Specialist referral is for anaphylaxis to a previous dose of the same vaccine or its components
explanation.pearls: Gelatin, not egg, is the component most often responsible for genuine anaphylaxis to measles, mumps and rubella or varicella vaccine, so a child who reacts to those vaccines should be assessed for gelatin allergy rather than re-tested to egg.

sources.label: ASCIA: Vaccination of the egg allergic child

subtopic_detail: Cyanosis with pulmonary venous congestion and a normal sized heart where prostaglandin does not help
stem:
You are the resident called to the special care nursery for a 2-day-old boy born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery after an uncomplicated pregnancy. The midwife says he has been grunting since the early hours and has gone from room air to needing help with his breathing.

He was started on nasal continuous positive airway pressure four hours ago and has deteriorated since, now needing 80 per cent oxygen with worsening subcostal recession. On 100 per cent oxygen delivered by head box for ten minutes his arterial oxygen tension rises only from 32 to 41 mmHg.

On examination he is dusky and tachypnoeic with a soft, quiet precordium and no murmur. The liver edge is palpable 4 cm below the costal margin. Femoral pulses are easily felt and equal to the brachial pulses. The chest radiograph shows a normal cardiac silhouette with diffuse fine granular opacification and prominent interstitial markings throughout both lung fields.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176/min, blood pressure 54/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 82/min, SpO2 76 per cent on 80 per cent oxygen, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Hyperoxia test: Arterial oxygen tension 32 mmHg in air rising only to 41 mmHg after 10 minutes of 100 per cent oxygen
data_table.Examination: Quiet precordium with no murmur, liver 4 cm below costal margin, femoral pulses equal to brachial
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph: normal cardiac silhouette, diffuse fine granular opacification and prominent interstitial markings bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Arterial pH 7.18, lactate 6.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), haemoglobin 178 g/L (140-220)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence a prostaglandin E1 infusion and arrange retrieval to a cardiac centre
options.rationale: Prostaglandin rescues lesions in which systemic or pulmonary blood flow depends on the duct, and it is the reflex answer to a failed hyperoxia test. Here the obstruction lies downstream of the lungs in the pulmonary venous pathway, so opening the duct increases pulmonary blood flow into an already congested circuit and can worsen the pulmonary oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Commence inhaled nitric oxide and arrange retrieval to a tertiary neonatal unit
options.rationale: Nitric oxide is the treatment for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, which usually follows meconium aspiration, sepsis or asphyxia and is supported by a pre-ductal to post-ductal saturation gradient. Given into an obstructed pulmonary venous pathway it increases transpulmonary flow against a fixed obstruction and precipitates frank pulmonary oedema. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Give surfactant, continue nasal continuous positive airway pressure and observe him
options.rationale: The granular radiographic appearance genuinely mimics surfactant deficiency, which is why this lesion is so often missed, but respiratory distress syndrome is a disease of prematurity and this baby is 39 weeks with no risk factors. Surfactant deficiency also responds to oxygen, whereas the hyperoxia test here failed outright. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Intubate and ventilate him, then arrange emergency retrieval for surgical repair
options.rationale: A term baby with a failed hyperoxia test, hepatomegaly, a quiet precordium and a normal sized heart with diffuse pulmonary venous congestion has obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage, in which no medical therapy relieves the obstruction. Intubation with positive pressure ventilation buys oxygenation and reduces the work of breathing while emergency surgical relief of the obstruction is arranged, and this is one of the few true surgical emergencies in neonatal cardiology. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin and arrange retrieval for review
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are appropriate alongside any neonatal deterioration and cultures should be taken, but sepsis does not explain a hyperoxia test that fails to lift the arterial oxygen tension above 100 mmHg. Treating this as sepsis alone delays the only intervention that works. (Source: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease

explanation.summary: Total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage returns oxygenated pulmonary venous blood to the right atrium rather than the left, so survival depends on an atrial communication and the clinical picture is set by whether the anomalous channel is obstructed. The infracardiac form, which descends through the diaphragm to the portal system, is the one most often obstructed, and it presents in the first days with profound cyanosis, severe respiratory distress and a chest radiograph showing pulmonary venous congestion over a heart of normal size. That combination of a small heart with wet lungs is the radiological signature and is the reason the lesion is repeatedly mistaken for respiratory distress syndrome, pneumonia or persistent pulmonary hypertension. The crucial management point is that the usual neonatal cardiac rescues make it worse: prostaglandin and nitric oxide both increase flow into a circuit that cannot drain, and extracorporeal support is not a substitute for relieving the obstruction. Definitive treatment is emergency surgical reimplantation of the pulmonary venous confluence into the left atrium.
key_points: A small heart with diffuse pulmonary venous congestion in a cyanosed term baby is the radiological signature
The hyperoxia test fails, but the obstruction is downstream of the lungs, not duct dependent
Prostaglandin and nitric oxide can both worsen obstructed anomalous pulmonary venous drainage
Hepatomegaly with a quiet precordium and no murmur is typical rather than reassuring
Definitive treatment is emergency surgery, so retrieval is arranged without waiting for stability
explanation.pearls: In obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage the murmur is usually absent because there is no turbulent flow across a valve or septal defect, so a silent precordium in a deeply cyanosed term baby should raise suspicion rather than lower it.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Cyanotic congenital heart disease
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network: Neonatal retrieval guidance
BMJ Best Practice: Total anomalous pulmonary venous connection

subtopic_detail: Feeding decision in a jaundiced septic neonate with positive urinary reducing substances and negative urine glucose
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting an 8-day-old exclusively breastfed girl. Her mother says she has been 'bringing up every feed' for four days, has gone floppy and sleepy, and has not soaked a nappy since yesterday.

She was born at term weighing 3400 g after an uncomplicated pregnancy and now weighs 3020 g. She is deeply jaundiced, lethargic and hypotonic with a capillary refill of 4 seconds. The liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin.

Blood cultures taken on arrival have flagged positive at 9 hours with Gram negative bacilli and intravenous cefotaxime has been given. Bedside testing shows a blood glucose of 1.9 mmol/L, which has been corrected with a glucose bolus. Bilirubin is predominantly conjugated and the international normalised ratio is prolonged. Urine tests positive for reducing substances while the urine glucose oxidase dipstick is negative. Newborn screening results have been requested but are not yet available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 184/min, blood pressure 58/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.2°C
data_table.Examination: Deep jaundice, lethargy, hypotonia, capillary refill 4 seconds, liver 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 268 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 96 micromol/L (less than 20), alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L (less than 45), international normalised ratio 2.4 (0.9-1.2), glucose 1.9 mmol/L before correction (2.6-6.0)
data_table.Urine: Reducing substances positive, glucose oxidase dipstick negative
data_table.Microbiology: Blood culture positive at 9 hours with Gram negative bacilli; intravenous cefotaxime given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her feeding?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and manage the sepsis with intravenous cefotaxime alone
options.rationale: Breast milk is the richest dietary source of lactose, and every further feed delivers the galactose that is driving the liver injury, the renal tubular dysfunction and the hypoglycaemia. Continuing to feed while treating only the infection leaves the underlying substrate load untouched. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and manage the sepsis with cefotaxime
options.rationale: Extensive hydrolysis alters the protein fraction to reduce allergenicity but most hydrolysed formulas still contain lactose, so the galactose exposure continues. The formula that treats cow milk protein allergy is not the formula that treats a galactose disorder. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate

options.text: Stop all lactose containing feeds, start soy formula and continue the cefotaxime
options.rationale: Positive urinary reducing substances with a negative glucose specific dipstick means a non-glucose reducing sugar, and galactosaemia presenting with conjugated jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia and Escherichia coli sepsis fits precisely. Lactose is withdrawn immediately and replaced with a soy based formula while confirmatory galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase assay and the newborn screening result are chased, because the biochemical injury reverses within days of removing the substrate. (Source: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate

options.text: Start ursodeoxycholic acid, continue breastfeeding and continue the cefotaxime
options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid is used for cholestasis of other causes such as biliary atresia awaiting surgery or parenteral nutrition associated liver disease, and it does nothing about an accumulating toxic metabolite. Treating the cholestasis symptomatically while the cause continues to be fed is the anti-pattern here. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

options.text: Start phenobarbitone, continue breastfeeding and continue the intravenous cefotaxime
options.rationale: Phenobarbitone induces hepatic enzymes and was historically used in hyperbilirubinaemia of other causes, and it is not a treatment for conjugated jaundice with coagulopathy. It would also sedate an already encephalopathic infant. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal jaundice)

explanation.summary: Classical galactosaemia results from galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency and presents in the first two weeks once milk feeding has begun, with vomiting, poor feeding, jaundice that becomes conjugated, hepatomegaly, coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia and renal tubular dysfunction. Its most characteristic association is Escherichia coli sepsis, which occurs because accumulated galactose-1-phosphate impairs neutrophil function, and a Gram negative septicaemia in a jaundiced neonate should always prompt the question. The bedside clue is a positive urinary reducing substance test alongside a negative glucose oxidase dipstick, since the dipstick is glucose specific while the reducing substance test detects galactose as well. Newborn screening includes galactosaemia in Australian programs but the result may not be available fast enough for a baby who is already unwell, so treatment is started on clinical suspicion. Lifelong lactose restriction prevents the acute liver and renal disease, although ovarian insufficiency and learning difficulties can still occur despite good dietary control.
key_points: Positive urinary reducing substances with a negative glucose dipstick indicates a non-glucose reducing sugar
Escherichia coli sepsis in a jaundiced neonate is the classic association of galactosaemia
Withdraw lactose immediately on clinical suspicion; do not wait for the screening result
Extensively hydrolysed formulas usually still contain lactose, so soy based formula is used
Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with coagulopathy in a neonate is always pathological
explanation.pearls: Soy formula is used in galactosaemia even though soy is otherwise avoided in infancy, because the galactose in soy is bound as raffinose and stachyose, which human infants cannot hydrolyse and therefore cannot absorb.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Metabolic disease in the neonate
Human Genetics Society of Australasia: Newborn bloodspot screening

subtopic_detail: Pharmacological lactation suppression after stillbirth in a normotensive woman
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar reviewing a 32-year-old woman on the ward. She gave birth two days ago at 34 weeks following an intrauterine foetal death, and is due for discharge tomorrow.

Her breasts have become firm, hot and painful overnight and milk is leaking through her clothing. She tells you she finds this 'unbearable to live with' and asks whether anything can be given to stop it. She has thought about donating milk and has decided against it.

Her blood pressure has been between 108/64 and 118/72 mmHg throughout the pregnancy and since birth, and her booking and postnatal blood pressure records contain no readings above 130/80 mmHg. She has no history of depression or psychosis, takes no regular medication and is not planning to feed a future infant in the coming weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1°C
data_table.Breast examination: Bilaterally firm, warm and tender with spontaneous leakage; no focal mass, no erythematous wedge, no fluctuance
data_table.History: Blood pressure never above 130/80 mmHg antenatally or postnatally; no psychiatric history; no regular medications

options.text: Prescribe bromocriptine 2.5 mg orally twice daily for a fourteen day course
options.rationale: Bromocriptine suppresses prolactin effectively but has been associated with hypertension, seizures, stroke and myocardial infarction in postpartum women, and it requires two weeks of twice daily dosing. Cabergoline has replaced it because a single dose achieves the same effect with a better safety profile. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe cabergoline 1 mg orally as a single dose with supportive breast measures
options.rationale: A single 1 mg oral dose of cabergoline is the Australian standard for lactation suppression after stillbirth or neonatal death, and it works best when given in the first days postpartum before full lactogenesis is established. Normal blood pressure throughout the pregnancy matters because hypertensive disorders and a psychotic illness history are the two main cautions against a dopamine agonist. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Prescribe oestrogen therapy for one week with firm breast support and ice packs
options.rationale: High dose oestrogen was used historically to suppress lactation but was abandoned because it substantially raises the risk of venous thromboembolism in an already prothrombotic postpartum period. This woman has an additional thrombotic risk from recent birth and reduced mobility. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

options.text: Advise firm breast support and analgesia alone and avoid any drug treatment
options.rationale: Non-pharmacological measures are always offered and are the right answer for a woman who declines medication, but engorgement managed this way takes one to two weeks to settle. Withholding an effective and safe option from a bereaved woman who has explicitly asked for it is not neutral. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

options.text: Advise regular expression of milk to comfort and review her again in one week
options.rationale: Regular expression stimulates prolactin release and maintains supply, which is the opposite of the goal here, and it is advised only for women who choose to express and donate. Minimal expression for comfort only is the correct non-pharmacological approach. (Source: RANZCOG: Stillbirth care)

explanation.summary: Lactogenesis proceeds after any birth beyond about 16 weeks gestation, so women who experience stillbirth, late miscarriage or neonatal death face the physical reminder of milk production during acute grief. Suppression is offered rather than assumed, because some women choose to express and donate milk as part of their grieving and that choice should be supported. When suppression is chosen, cabergoline given as a single 1 mg oral dose is the Australian first-line agent, most effective within the first few days postpartum. Blood pressure should be checked first, as dopamine agonists are avoided in uncontrolled hypertension and in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and there is a recognised though uncommon association with psychotic symptoms. Supportive measures continue alongside the drug: a firm supportive bra, cold packs, simple analgesia and minimal expression for comfort only.
key_points: Cabergoline 1 mg orally as a single dose is the Australian first-line suppressant
It works best in the first days postpartum before lactation is fully established
Check blood pressure first; avoid dopamine agonists in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Bromocriptine and oestrogen have both been abandoned on safety grounds
Offer suppression rather than assume it, as some women choose to express and donate
explanation.pearls: Cabergoline has a terminal half-life of around 60 hours, which is why one 1 mg dose suppresses prolactin for two to three weeks while bromocriptine needed twice daily dosing for a fortnight.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Lactation suppression
